explanations.explanation: This neuron flags tokens written in non-Latin scripts (e.g. Hangul, Kanji/Kana, Devanagari, Arabic, Chinese characters, etc.), activating whenever the text contains characters outside the basic Latin alphabet.

This feature lights up on the repetitive “boilerplate” metadata and structural text you find in web-pages and docs—copyright notices, license disclaimers, “all rights reserved,” RSS/social-media links, “last edited/posted on” stamps, placeholder page notices, etc. It’s essentially picking out the template-driven footer/metadata chunks rather than the main content.
This neuron fires on enumeration markers—i.e. the numbers or ordinals that head off list items or sectional headings in structured, numbered lists.
This feature fires on the equative/comparative “just as … as …” construction—that is, the subordinating “as” used to mark an emphatic equivalence between two items.

This neuron detects speaker-stance markers—those little hedges, fillers and polite/modal words (like “like,” “sorry for…,” “had,” “could,” “would,” “hopefully,” etc.) that soften or qualify an utterance.

This neuron is basically a “rare‐token” detector – it fires whenever the model sees an infrequent or out‐of‐ordinary piece of text (e.g. odd Unicode or HTML‐entity fragments like “&#82”, replacement‐chars, stars, bullets, or low‐frequency subword bits such as “cop,” “illi,” “rom,” etc.).
This feature flags the very first token of a new text segment (e.g. the opening word of an article, section, or paragraph), especially a capitalized lead‐in.

This feature is a general “boundary detector” – it lights up wherever the model is entering a new chunk, whether that’s the second subword of a compound, the infinitival to of a verb, a list-introducing phrase (such as), a hyphenated break, or even the very first token of a heading or section.

The common thread is that this neuron lights up on the subword “cores” of long, formal, often Latinate or technical words right at their start (discontin-, schol-, grav-, subpo-, hyp-, burg-, etc.). In other words, it detects the prefixes of multi-syllabic, content‐heavy terms typical of legal, academic or specialized prose.

This neuron is basically a “PP-starter” detector—it lights up on the preposition “in” when it begins a prepositional phrase (e.g. “in my shop,” “in the world,” “in a blender,” “in between,” “in moderation,” etc.).
This neuron fires on the “.” token—whether it’s a sentence-ending period or the decimal point in numbers.

Here’s a concise concept summary for each high‐activation feature, in the order you gave them:

1. (≈1.000) Detection of adult/pornographic advertisement text and URLs (e.g. “18 sexy.biz … find love or girlfriend…”).  
2. (≈0.862) Plain, factual single‐sentence scene descriptions in English (“The umbrella is next to the window,” “It’s getting cold now”).  
3. (≈0.862) Promotional product‐spec copy highlighting physical features (e.g. “High Quality Deep Bass Sound,” “waterproof Bluetooth Speaker”).  
4. (≈0.815) Bibliographic or publication metadata entries in East Asian scripts (dates, ISBNs, publishers).  
5. (≈0.327–0.513) Numbered moral aphorisms or religious sayings formatted as a list (e.g. “1. Good does not perish,” parallel Arabic hadith lines).  
6. (unlabeled) Professional biography/CV‐style text for hospitality staff (“The Food & Beverage Manager of the Hotel Carlsbad Plaza…”).  
7. (≈0.736) Music track listings and streaming‐service links (artist – track title, Spotify/playlist URLs).  
8. (≈0.734) Formal organization names and acronyms in Cyrillic (e.g. “MCRSI – International Center for Development of Social Initiatives,” with .ru domain).  
9. (≈0.728) Arabic‐language hotel or resort descriptions (amenities, star rating, location details).  
10. (unlabeled) Structured “Subject:” headings for article sections, especially religious or academic topics (“Subject: Hadith (Shiites), Subject: Poetry – Religious aspects”).  
11. (unlabeled) Encyclopedic entries for animal species, common and scientific names with taxonomy details.  
12. (≈0.662) Ethnographic or anthropological habitat descriptions listing indigenous place‐names in local languages.  
13. (unlabeled) Encyclopedic place entry for a capital city, with historical names, dynastic periods, pronunciation notes.  
14. (unlabeled) Descriptions of digital accessibility platforms for hearing‐impaired users (sign‐language/video/text display).  
15. (unlabeled) Celebrity biography entries (birth name, date, career milestones for an actress/singer).  
16. (unlabeled) Film or biographical article blurbs about real‐life criminals/drug traffickers (“The True Story Of George Jung…”).  
17. (≈0.619) Advertising copy for home‐hardware fixtures with manufacturer details (“Wolff Design Center … floor register by Barclay”).  
18. (unlabeled) Legal copyright and trademark notices (“Copyright 2016 by M̊ns Greb̊ck. All rights reserved. Melay Script is a trademark…”).  
19. (unlabeled) News‐style reporting on medical research or vaccine clinical trials, with institutional affiliations and statistics.  
20. (≈0.397) Informal food‐blog or brand‐partnership posts (“By Nick…Carvel’s recent partnership with Nutella…call 2014 the year of the hazelnut”).

This neuron appears to be a generic BPE‐subword detector: it lights up on common internal word fragments or symbols (e.g. “susp” in suspension, “if” in beautiful, “we” in tweets, “emer” in emergency, “der” in Hyderabad, “read” in dreadlocks, “eng” in Hengl, “il” in silk, “ken” in taken, “/” as a separator, etc.), regardless of the larger context.
This neuron fires at the full‐stop that closes off a heading or title—i.e. it detects the boundary between a headline (or named label) and the start of the following descriptive text.

This neuron is essentially a “new‐line/new‐segment” detector.  It spikes on tokens that begin a post, paragraph, heading or quoted block—greetings, dates, titles or any line-initial word or symbol—marking sentence-/segment-start positions.

This feature detects the “linker” element in symmetrical or range‐style constructions—i.e. the punctuation or preposition (slashes “/”, ampersands “&”, or the word “to”) that joins two identical units (e.g. day-to-day, 2010/11, A&B) to mark a repeated or ranged expression.

This feature fires on non‐alphanumeric, decorative Unicode glyphs—emojis, stars, bullets, bars and other ornamental/separator symbols—used to stylize or delimit content in user‐generated and formatted text.
This feature is highly selective for “internal” periods that close off abbreviations, acronyms, initials or similar non-sentence-final markers (e.g. “Oct.”, “U.S.”, “LLC.”, “Room A.”).
This neuron is simply a “dot‐detector”: it fires strongly on the period token (the full stop), marking sentence ends, abbreviations (e.g. “Inc.”, “Drs.”), decimal points, etc.
This feature is simply the “dot” punctuation token (“.”), whether used as a sentence‐ending full stop, an abbreviation marker, a decimal point or in domain names.
